steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have imported React and useState, making them available for use in your component.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState, which are essential for building React components with state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check your import statement. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX. The component should be typed to return JSX.Element.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Make sure to include the return statement with some JSX content.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and ready to be used as the main entry point.
successCriteria: Component named 'App' exists
Component returns JSX
Component has proper TypeScript typing
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your component is named 'App', returns JSX, and has proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a functional component named App that returns JSX with TypeScript typing.

steps.title: Initialize search input state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'search' with an initial value of an empty string.
steps.hint: Remember to use the useState hook you imported earlier. The syntax is: const [search, setSearch] = useState<string>('');
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a string state variable
const [username, setUsername] = useState<string>('');
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a search state variable initialized with an empty string value inside your App component.
successCriteria: The code must include a useState call that creates a 'search' state variable with an initial empty string value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the search state variable. This will track the user's input as they type in the search field.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're creating a state variable called 'search' with an initial empty string value using useState.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'search' with an initial value of an empty string.

steps.title: Initialize debounced search state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a second state variable called 'debouncedSearch' using useState, initialized with an empty string.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook again, just like you did for the search input state. The type will be inferred as string from the initial value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of creating a second state variable
const [filteredValue, setFilteredValue] = useState('');
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will now have two separate state variables: 'search' for the immediate input and 'debouncedSearch' for the delayed version.
successCriteria: The code should include a second useState call that declares a variable named 'debouncedSearch' with an initial empty string value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a separate state variable to hold the debounced version of the search input. This is essential for implementing the debounce pattern.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're creating a state variable specifically named 'debouncedSearch' with an initial empty string value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on creating just the debouncedSearch state variable. Use useState with an empty string initial value, similar to how you created the search state.

steps.title: Create the useDebounce custom hook
steps.instruction: Create a custom hook function named 'useDebounce' that takes two parameters: 'value' of generic type T, and 'delay' of type number. The function should return a value of type T. Place this function outside of your App component.
steps.hint: Define a function with the signature 'function useDebounce<T>(value: T, delay: number): T'. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a 'useDebounce' function defined with proper TypeScript generics that can accept any type of value and a delay number, returning the same type.
successCriteria: The code must contain a function named 'useDebounce' with two parameters (value of generic type T, delay of type number) and a return type of T.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the useDebounce custom hook with TypeScript generics. This provides a type-safe foundation for the debouncing logic we'll implement next.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your function signature. Make sure you have: 1) The function is named 'useDebounce', 2) It takes two parameters (value with generic type T, delay as number), 3) It returns type T.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useDebounce function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function named 'useDebounce' that accepts a value (with generic type T) and a delay (number), and returns the same type T.

steps.title: Add state to track debounced value in the hook
steps.instruction: Inside the useDebounce custom hook, use useState to create a state variable called debouncedValue. Initialize it with the initial value passed to the hook.
steps.hint: Add const [debouncedValue, setDebouncedValue] = useState<T>(value) inside the useDebounce function body.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useDebounce hook now has internal state to store the debounced value.
successCriteria: useState is called inside useDebounce
state variable is named debouncedValue
state is initialized with the value parameter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added state inside the custom hook to track the debounced value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState inside useDebounce, naming the variable debouncedValue, and initializing it with the value parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on adding state inside the useDebounce hook. Use useState to create a debouncedValue state variable initialized with the value parameter.

steps.title: Add useEffect to implement debouncing logic
steps.instruction: Inside the useDebounce hook, import useEffect from 'react' and add a useEffect that sets a timeout to update the debouncedValue state after the specified delay.
steps.hint: Remember to clear the previous timeout when the value or delay changes to avoid memory leaks.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useDebounce hook now includes a useEffect that creates a timer to update debouncedValue after the specified delay, with proper cleanup.
successCriteria: The useEffect hook should be imported and implemented with setTimeout to update debouncedValue, include a cleanup function, and have the correct dependency array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the debouncing logic with useEffect. The timer will update the debounced value after the specified delay, and the cleanup function prevents memory leaks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if you've included all necessary parts: useEffect import, setTimeout to update debouncedValue, cleanup function with clearTimeout, and proper dependency array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect implementation is missing or incorrect. Remember to import useEffect, set a timeout to update debouncedValue, return a cleanup function, and include value and delay in dependencies.

steps.title: Add cleanup function to clear timeout
steps.instruction: Inside the useEffect in your useDebounce hook, return a cleanup function that clears the timeout using clearTimeout.
steps.hint: The cleanup function should run when the component unmounts or before the effect runs again. Use clearTimeout with the timeout ID stored from setTimeout.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect will have a cleanup function that prevents memory leaks by clearing the timeout when dependencies change or the component unmounts.
successCriteria: The useEffect returns a function
The returned function calls clearTimeout
clearTimeout is called with the timeout ID
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the cleanup function to clear the timeout, which prevents memory leaks when the component unmounts or the value changes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your useEffect returns a cleanup function that calls clearTimeout with the correct timeout ID.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect should return a cleanup function that clears the timeout. Try adding `return () => { clearTimeout(timerId); };` inside useEffect.

steps.title: Return the debounced value from the hook
steps.instruction: Return the debouncedValue state from the useDebounce hook so components can use it.
steps.hint: At the end of your useDebounce function, return the debouncedValue variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useDebounce hook now returns the debouncedValue state, making it available to any component that calls the hook.
successCriteria: The useDebounce function should return the debouncedValue variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully returned the debounced value from the hook. This makes the debounced value available to any component that uses this custom hook.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but the hook isn't returning the debounced value yet. Make sure to return the debouncedValue variable at the end of the useDebounce function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useDebounce hook should return the debouncedValue state. Check that you're returning the correct variable from the function.

steps.title: Use the useDebounce hook in the App component
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, call the useDebounce hook with the search state and a delay of 500 milliseconds.
steps.hint: Call the hook like this: useDebounce(search, 500) and store its return value in a variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of using a custom hook
const debouncedValue = useDebounce(inputValue, 300);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a variable storing the debounced version of the search input.
successCriteria: useDebounce
search
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully called the useDebounce hook with the search state and a 500ms delay.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're calling useDebounce with the search variable and the number 500 as arguments.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook call is missing or incorrect. You need to call useDebounce(search, 500) inside the App component.

steps.title: Create search input and wire it to state
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, add an input element with its value bound to the search state and an onChange handler that updates the search state.
steps.hint: Use the onChange event to call setSearch with the input's current value. The value attribute should be set to the search state variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will render a text input that updates the search state as the user types.
successCriteria: Input element with type="text"
value attribute bound to search state
onChange handler that calls setSearch with e.target.value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created an input that updates the search state on every keystroke.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the input's value is bound to the search state and the onChange handler updates it correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input isn't properly wired to the search state. Check that you're using the search variable for value and setSearch in the onChange handler.

steps.title: Display both current and debounced values
steps.instruction:
Inside the App component's return statement, add two paragraph elements (

) to display both the current search value and the debounced search value. Show the current value with a label like 'Current search:' and the debounced value with a label like 'Debounced search:'.
steps.hint:
Use JSX curly braces to embed the state values. For example:

Current search: {search}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show both the immediate search value and the debounced value, demonstrating how debouncing delays updates.
successCriteria:
Two

elements are added inside the return statement
First paragraph displays 'Current search: {search}'
Second paragraph displays 'Debounced search: {debouncedSearch}'
Values are correctly referenced using curly braces
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added visual feedback showing both the immediate and debounced values. This demonstrates the core concept of debouncing in action.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both paragraphs with proper labels and correctly referenced state values.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've added two paragraph elements inside the return statement, each displaying one of the state values with appropriate labels.
